passage:
Biology teacher's note, Class 10 health session.
Today we covered consent, boundaries and sexual health. The class was giggly at first. I kept it factual: consent means a clear, free yes; it can be taken back at any time; silence or pressure is not a yes.
Sahil asked, "What if someone says yes and then changes their mind?" I said then it's a no, and a respectful person stops. Uma added, "Like when my cousin tickles me and I say stop, and he doesn't. That's annoying, and it's also not okay." The class went quiet, then nodded.
We also covered how infections and pregnancy can be prevented, and that a doctor or the school nurse can give confidential, accurate advice.
Next week: an anonymous question box. — Mrs Thomas

qa.q: What will Mrs Thomas set up next week?
qa.a: An anonymous question box.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling when he asked his question?
qa.a: Sahil was probably curious and a bit unsure, wanting to understand what happens if someone changes their mind.

qa.q: Why is an anonymous question box a good next step?
qa.a: It lets students ask embarrassing questions safely and get accurate answers instead of myths.

qa.q: How might Uma's classmates see consent after her example?
qa.a: They may see that consent applies to everyday touch too, and that "stop" should always be respected.

grounding: A teacher's note records a factual class session on consent and sexual health.

Dear Diary,
At Rukhsar's birthday party tonight, Yusuf and I were talking on the balcony. It was nice. Then he leaned in like he wanted to kiss me.
I froze. I like him, but I wasn't ready. My heart was pounding.
I said, "Not now. I'm not comfortable."
He stepped back straight away. He said, "Okay. Sorry. Thanks for telling me." And then he just kept talking about the cricket match, like it was normal.
I thought he'd be angry or sulk. He didn't. I actually like him more now.
I'm glad I said it. And I'm glad he listened.
— Afreen

qa.a: Afreen felt nervous and unsure, liking Yusuf but not ready.

qa.a: Yusuf may feel a little awkward or disappointed, but he respects Afreen, so he stays friendly.

During exam week, Pema's phone was always buzzing. It was Advait, her boyfriend. "Where are you?" "Who's that in your story?" "Share your location."
At first she thought it meant he cared. Then, on Wednesday, she left her phone at home by mistake. When she got back there were thirty messages and a voice note: "Why are you ignoring me? Are you with someone?"
Her friend Parul read them over her shoulder. "Pema… this isn't caring. This is checking."
Pema felt sick. She thought of how she'd stopped going to the library with the study group because Advait didn't like it.
That evening she showed the messages to her mother. Her mother listened, then said, "You deserve someone who trusts you. Whatever you decide, I'm with you. Let's talk to your class counsellor tomorrow too."

qa.q: How many messages were waiting when Pema got back?
qa.a: Thirty messages.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when Parul said "This is checking"?
qa.a: Pema felt sick and shaken, starting to see the messages as control, not care.

qa.q: What steps did Pema take that others could learn from?
qa.a: She listened to a friend's concern, noticed how her own life had shrunk, and showed the messages to her mother the same day.

qa.q: How does Parul see Advait's messages?
qa.a: Parul sees them as checking and control, not love, and says so gently.

grounding: A teen recognises a partner's constant checking as control and tells her mother.

Trisha eats lunch alone every day with a book. Her class teacher asked me to check if she was lonely.
I met her today. She said, "I like it. The canteen is so loud. I get to read and recharge." She has two close friends she sees after school. She seemed calm and cheerful.

The stream choice form was due at noon, and it was already eleven. Kiran stood outside the school office, pen in hand.
Her mother, Rajni, was on the phone from the hospital where she worked. "Beta, you're good at biology. You could be a doctor."
"Ma, I'm good at it. But I love computers. I built the school website."
The office clerk tapped her watch.
Rajni paused. "Which one do you think about when you're free?"
"Computers. Always."
"Then choose the stream that keeps both open. Take maths with computer science. Talk to your teacher about biology as an extra."
Kiran ticked the box at 11:52 and handed it in, hands shaking. Rajni said, "Call me after. I'm proud of you."

qa.a: At noon.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when she handed in the form?
qa.a: Kiran felt nervous and relieved, with her hands shaking.

qa.q: What question from Rajni helped Kiran decide?
qa.a: Asking which subject Kiran thinks about when free helped her see her real interest.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel after the call?
qa.a: Rajni probably feels proud and a little relieved that Kiran chose thoughtfully.

grounding: Under a deadline a teen and her mother weigh interests and expectations in choosing a stream.

Hafsa was selling her old cycle online. A buyer messaged: "I'll pay now. Just scan this QR code to receive the money."
She was in a rush; her bus was due and the buyer kept messaging: "Quick, or I'll buy another one."
Hafsa opened the scanner. Then her friend Gargi grabbed her arm. "Wait. You never scan to receive money. Scanning is for paying."
Hafsa looked. The screen said "Pay Rs 4,500". Her heart jumped.
"That would've taken money from my account!"
She blocked the buyer, took a screenshot and reported it on the cyber crime helpline, 1930, with her father that evening. Then she added a note in her phone: "Receiving money = no scan, no PIN."

qa.q: What did the screen say when Hafsa opened the scanner?
What was Hafsa feeling when her heart jumped?
qa.a: Hafsa felt shocked and scared, realising she almost lost money.

qa.q: What steps did Hafsa take after spotting the scam?
qa.a: She blocked the buyer, took a screenshot, and reported it with her father on the cyber crime helpline.

qa.q: How does Gargi see the QR code request?
qa.a: Gargi sees it as a scam because scanning is for paying, not receiving.

grounding: Under time pressure a teen nearly falls for a QR code scam, spots it and reports it.

Every month Hansa got her pocket money into her own bank account, linked to her phone. And every month, by the 20th, it was gone.
"Where does it go?" asked her father, Santosh.
Hansa shrugged. "Snacks? Stuff?"
So Santosh suggested she track it. For one month, Hansa wrote every payment in a notes app: canteen, auto, a phone cover, gifts.
At the end she was shocked. Almost half went on canteen snacks and small online orders she didn't even remember.
She made three columns: needs, wants, saving. She didn't stop the snacks, but she cut the small orders. Next month, she still had some left on the 30th.
She showed Santosh the notes. He grinned. "You're better at this than me."

qa.q: By which date was Hansa's pocket money usually gone?
qa.a: By the 20th.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she saw where the money went?
qa.a: Hansa felt shocked and a little embarrassed at how much went on things she didn't remember.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that helped her keep track?
qa.a: She wrote down every payment for a month, then sorted spending into needs, wants and saving.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Hansa's tracking?
qa.a: Santosh is proud and impressed, even joking she's better at it than him.

grounding: A teen tracks her digital payments to understand her spending and make a simple budget.

"Aditi, my payment app is showing an error. I called customer care," said Deepak, her brother, holding his phone.
"Where did you get the number?"
"Online. The first search result."
Aditi frowned. "What did they say?"
"They said to share the OTP so they can fix it."
"Don't! Real companies never ask for OTPs."
"But he sounded so official."
"That's the trick. Hang up."
Deepak hung up, hands trembling. "I almost told him."
Aditi opened the official app and found the real help section. "Always use the app itself, not a search result."
They told their mother that evening and reported the number to the cyber crime helpline together.

qa.q: Where did Deepak find the customer care number?
qa.a: The first search result online.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when his hands were trembling?
qa.a: Deepak felt shaken and scared, realising how close he came to sharing the OTP.

qa.q: What did Aditi teach Deepak about getting help?
qa.a: Never share an OTP, and use the official app's help section instead of a search result.

qa.q: How does Aditi see the caller?
qa.a: Aditi sees the official-sounding voice as part of the scam, not a sign of a real company.

grounding: A teen stops her brother from sharing an OTP with fake customer care and they report it.

I'm Harish, and I sat next to Rajni in the Class 11 common room when a video went round the group: "Breaking: Voting date changed, go vote tomorrow instead!"
Rajni's grandmother was going to vote. Rajni frowned and didn't forward it. She opened the Election Commission website on her phone, scrolled, and said, "The date is the same. This is fake."
Then she typed in the group: "Checked the official site. Date hasn't changed. Please don't forward."
A few people reacted with thumbs up. One person said she was being preachy.
I don't know if she was angry or just worried about her Nani. But she stayed calm and posted the link.

qa.q: Which website did Rajni check?
qa.a: The Election Commission website.

qa.q: What might Rajni have been feeling when she frowned at the video?
qa.a: Rajni was probably worried and suspicious, thinking of her grandmother who planned to vote.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She didn't forward the video, checked the official source, and shared the correct link calmly.

qa.q: How does Harish see Rajni's reaction?
qa.a: Harish can't tell exactly how Rajni feels but sees her stay calm and use facts.

grounding: A classmate watches a teen check a false voting claim against the official source.

Before: In July, Kunal didn't care about the school council election. "It's a popularity contest," he said. Reena, who was running, asked him to at least read the manifestos.

Varun, you're asking why I get so serious about voting. Let me tell you about my first time.
I was nineteen. Someone in the market said, "If you vote for the wrong party, your ration card will be cancelled." Everyone believed it. I was scared.
I went to our teacher, Master-ji. He said, "Your vote is secret. Nobody can know. And no party can cancel your card for how you voted." He showed me the rules in a book.
So I voted. For the one I thought would fix our road. That party lost. But the road got fixed anyway, two years later.
Your Bhupen dada learned: check the rumour, then vote without fear.

qa.q: What did someone in the market say would happen if you voted for the wrong party?
qa.a: Your ration card will be cancelled.

qa.q: What was young Bhupen feeling after hearing the rumour?
qa.a: Bhupen felt scared that his vote could cost the family the ration card.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped young Bhupen vote without fear?
qa.a: He chose to check the rumour with Master-ji, who showed him the rules about the secret ballot.

qa.q: How might Master-ji have felt helping young Bhupen?
qa.a: Master-ji probably felt glad to clear up the rumour and help a young person vote.

grounding: A grandfather tells how he checked a voting rumour before his first vote.
